newsitem.title: USA: Port of Miami credit not threatened by scandal.
newsitem.headline: Port of Miami credit not threatened by scandal.

text.p: Recently discovered deficits and questionable spending at the Port of Miami are unlikely to affect the Florida seaport's bonds, Dade County officials and rating analysts said.
"All of the debt is insured," Dade County Finance Director Rachel Baum said.

The seaport has about $272 million of bond debt. All are revenue bonds except for a $142 million issue that is repaid from port revenues, but carries a backup general obligation pledge from Dade County, which runs the seaport.

County commissioners discovered last month that the port, a semi-autonomous agency they believed to be profitable, had a $22 million cash flow deficit and had borrowed $37 million from the county general fund over several years.

Port Director Carmen Lunetta abruptly announced his retirement after a port contractor released records showing seaport revenues had been used for questionable expenditures including Super Bowl tickets, campaign contributions to county commissioners, and luxury car leases.

MBIA Inc, which insures the bulk of the seaport debt through its bond insurer MBIA Insurance Corp., said most of those problems were political, and were not a credit threat. County commissioners approved some of that spending, MBIA Vice President Cheryl May noted.
"The port itself is very strong. It's a gateway to Latin America. It's in a very strong market position. There's very good debt service coverage," May said.
She said the transfers from the general fund were not a concern because the port has adequate revenues to repay the money.
Additionally, May said, "Concerns about running in the red were based on depreciation as an expense. That's really a non-cash item. Basically the port has been financially healthy."
The seaport has no underlying ratings, but Dade County's general obligation bonds are rated A1 by Moody's Investors Service Inc and A-plus by Fitch Investors Service Inc.
"We have no intentions at this time of taking any rating action," said John Incorvaia, a vice president with Moody's.
"We monitor the insured portfolio to make sure they have the ability to repay and that there's no violation of bond covenants. We don't see any of that at this point of time." Incorvaia said.
Andrea Bozzo, a managing director at Fitch, said that agency also saw no cause for alarm.
Incorvaia said Moody's had concerns about the county's monitoring system and the initial lack of a formal repayment schedule for general fund money loaned to the port.
However, he said, "At the present time we're satisfied that they (the county) have taken the appropraite action and that there's been no serious financial impact for the county."
Dade County budget analyst Peter Velar said the seaport has worked out a schedule to repay the money borrowed from the Dade general fund.
In three-and-a-half years they should be out of the hole," Velar said.

County budget analysts also said there was no danger of the port failing to make debt service payments. The seaport budget for fiscal 1997 is about $100 million, including $17 million for debt service. Additionally, the port has $20.4 million of cash reserves for debt service.
